claim: SCNR computes the scanner-left world-X XTEMP = BGL − ($8000 − 150*32) = BGL − $6D40; every blip is measured from it.
The blip loop subtracts XTEMP from the object's world X with a 16-bit SUBD, so the projection is modular in the $10000 world cylinder — that modular subtract IS the radar wrap seam.
SCNR reads the object's ABSOLUTE 16-bit world X (OX16) — not an on-screen coordinate — so off-camera attackers still project onto the radar.
The camera-relative position's high byte is shifted right twice (LSRA×2), compressing the 16-bit difference to a 6-bit radar column: (D>>8)>>2 = D>>10.

source.verbatim: SCNR2	LSRA		SHIFT DOWN TO 6 BITS

claim: The scanner strip is 64 columns wide: the terrain-erase loop terminates at (SCANER!>8)+64.
The object's Y is shifted right three times (LSRB×3) to the radar row: y >> 3.
A blip carries the object's colour word OBJCOL — a palette index — stored verbatim into the scanner, never a fresh colour.

The scanner bezel mark is the byte $9090 — palette index 9 (WHITE) in its high nibble — that the MTX bezel routine (*SCANNER BEZEL, :1225-1233) stores into the SCANH scanner addresses to frame the radar strip's ends. df7-5's BEZEL_COLOUR=9 is this nibble; the frame is a pair of end-brackets, not a full-width bar.

The scanner PLAYER BLIP is on a SEPARATE path from the SCNR world-attacker loop (*PLAYER BLIP OUTPUT, :1242-1258): it loads PLAXC — the player's fixed SCREEN position — and derives the marker's radar column (A>>4, :1243-1246) and row (B>>3, :1247-1249) from it, with NO camera (XTEMP) subtraction. So the player marker is camera-INVARIANT: it holds its radar column as the world scrolls, unlike an attacker blip (SUBD XTEMP, :1261). df7-8 re-derives this to our centred strip by projecting the player's own world position.

The player marker written into the scanner is the byte $9099 — palette index 9 (WHITE) in its high nibble, the same index-9 white as the bezel ($9090, :1227). df7-8's player blip draws by this palette INDEX, never a fresh colour.
